sentences.text: Platecarpus is distinguished by a short skull and a reduced number of teeth compared to other mosasaurs, possessing only about ten teeth in each lower jaw.
A preserved section of the digestive tract in one specimen contained the remains of mid-sized fish.
Fossil material within the scleral ring of a complete skeleton may represent the actual retina of the eye.
An exceptionally preserved individual shows skin impressions, nasal pigment, and bronchial tubes alongside a high caudal fin.
The genus Platecarpus was first described by Edward Drinker Cope in the year 1869.
Although several fossil skeletons have been found in Kansas deposits, researchers have recovered only one complete skull for this animal.
Evidence from a well-preserved specimen indicates Platecarpus ate moderate-sized fish, while hypotheses suggest it also consumed squid and ammonites.
Platecarpus had less robust teeth than tylosaurs, suggesting it fed on smaller or softer prey like small fish and squid.
Platecarpus likely fed on fish, squid, and ammonites.
Isotopic analysis of teeth suggests Platecarpus may have occasionally entered freshwater environments, similar to modern sea snakes.
Undigested scales and bones in the colon suggest Platecarpus processed food quickly without fully digesting or absorbing it.
Research suggests Platecarpus swam with powerful, fast movements similar to modern sharks rather than in an eel-like fashion.
Platecarpus likely swam using a shark-like method rather than the eel-like lateral undulation typical of other mosasaurs.
The downturned caudal vertebrae indicate that Platecarpus possessed a crescent-shaped tail fluke.
Platecarpus utilized carangiform locomotion, where the tail base remained stable while the fluke and back undulated.

While it was traditionally thought that mosasaurs propelled themselves through water with a lateral body undulation similar to eels or sea snakes, the large tail fin of Platecarpus suggests it swam more like a shark.
This swimming method is known as carangiform locomotion.
Platecarpus had a long downward-pointing tail with a large dorsal lobe, steering fins, and jaws with aligned conical teeth.
Platecarpus grew up to 4.3 meters in length, with the tail occupying half of that length.
A complete specimen indicates Platecarpus reached lengths of 5.57 to 5.67 meters and weighed approximately 548 kilograms.
Neural spines on these vertebrae had grooves for the insertion of interspinous ligaments and dorsal connective tissues which may have helped in the lateral movement of the fin.
Platecarpus belongs to the family Mosasauridae.
Scientists now consider Platecarpus to be a paraphyletic genus.
Later studies indicate that Platecarpus is a paraphyletic genus.
Platecarpus is considered monotypic because P. coryphaeus and P. ictericus were synonymized with the type species P. tympaniticus.
Platecarpus fossils date to the Late Cretaceous, with a possible record from the late Campanian.
Platecarpus fossils are found in Smoky Hill Chalk rocks dating from the late Santonian to the early Campanian.
Platecarpus lived during the Late Cretaceous.
Platecarpus lived approximately 84 to 81 million years ago at the end of the Cretaceous period.
Fossils of Platecarpus have been found in the United States, and possibly in Belgium, Australia, and Africa.
It is debated whether Platecarpus swam like an eel or like a modern shark, with recent studies favoring the latter.
